title: Con tacto
subtitle: Tactful criticism, delicate news & conflict resolution

lessons.title: Giving criticism tactfully
lessons.goal: Raise a delicate issue with a colleague constructively, without causing offence.

tip.title: Soft on the person, clear on the issue
tip.body: Start with genuine appreciation, describe what you observed (He notado que…) instead of judging, and ask for the other person's view (¿Tú cómo lo ves?). Spanish softens with tenses: the imperfect (Quería comentarte algo) and the conditional (¿Qué necesitarías…?, ¿Te importaría…?) sound gentler than the present. Me habría gustado que + imperfect subjunctive expresses a wish about the past without accusing anyone. Speak a little more slowly and warmly than usual: the melody matters as much as the words.

phrases.t: Valoro mucho tu compromiso, por eso quería hablarlo contigo abiertamente.
phrases.n: I really value your commitment, which is why I wanted to talk about it with you openly.

phrases.t: He notado que últimamente los plazos se han ido retrasando un poco.

phrases.t: ¿Te importaría enviar los informes un poco antes a partir de ahora?

phrases.t: En general, tu trabajo me parece excelente.

lessons.title: Resolving a conflict
lessons.goal: De-escalate a heated situation and negotiate a fair compromise.

tip.title: Calm voice, common ground
tip.body: First acknowledge the other person's feelings (Entiendo perfectamente que le moleste; entender que + subjunctive here, because you accept the feeling rather than state a fact), then separate the person from the problem (No se trata de buscar culpables, sino de…) and look for room to move (margen de maniobra, un término medio). Siempre y cuando + subjunctive lets you agree on a condition. In a conflict, consciously lower your pitch and speed: a calm, low voice de-escalates more than any argument. Neighbours in Argentina often say vos to each other, but with an older neighbour usted is the safe choice.

phrases.t: Entiendo perfectamente que le moleste.

lines.name: Don Ricardo
lines.t: ¡Otra vez! Tengo una mancha de humedad enorme en el techo del baño, y viene de su departamento.
lines.n: Again! I've got a huge damp patch on my bathroom ceiling, and it's coming from your flat.
lines.note: Argentina, Mexico: el departamento; Spain: el piso.

lines.t: Entiendo perfectamente que le moleste. Parece que ha habido un malentendido: yo no sabía nada de la mancha.
lines.n: I completely understand that it bothers you. It seems there's been a misunderstanding: I didn't know anything about the patch.

lines.name: Don Ricardo
lines.t: ¿Cómo que no sabía? ¡Hace dos semanas que le dejé una nota debajo de la puerta!
lines.n: What do you mean you didn't know? I left you a note under the door two weeks ago!

lines.t: No la vi, de verdad. Pero no se trata de buscar culpables, sino de encontrar una solución. Mañana mismo llamo a un plomero.
lines.n: I didn't see it, honestly. But it's not about finding someone to blame, but about finding a solution. I'll call a plumber first thing tomorrow.
lines.note: Latin America: el plomero; Spain: el fontanero.

lines.name: Don Ricardo
lines.t: ¿Y la pintura del techo, quién la paga? Porque yo no pienso pagarla, eh.
lines.n: And who pays for painting the ceiling? Because I'm not paying for it, you know.

lines.t: ¿Podríamos llegar a un término medio? Yo pago el arreglo de la cañería y pedimos que el seguro del consorcio cubra la pintura. Siempre y cuando esté de acuerdo, lo dejamos por escrito.
lines.n: Could we reach a middle ground? I'll pay for the pipe repair and we'll ask the building's insurance to cover the painting. Provided you agree, we'll put it in writing.
lines.note: Argentina: el consorcio = the building's owners' association; Spain: la comunidad de propietarios.

lessons.title: Saying no diplomatically
lessons.goal: Turn down a request without burning bridges and offer an alternative.

tip.title: Never a bare no
tip.body: In professional Spanish a refusal is wrapped: express regret (Me temo que…, Lamentablemente…), give a reason, then open a door (¿Me permite hacerle una contrapropuesta?, Lo que sí podríamos hacer es…). Impersonal phrasing such as no va a ser viable or tal como está planteado depersonalises the problem, so the no is about the plan, not the person. Tener las manos atadas (to have your hands tied) shows the decision isn't yours. In Colombia usted is used very widely, even in friendly business relationships. Keep a friendly, steady tone so the no sounds final but not hostile.

phrases.n: I understand your request, but unfortunately our hands are tied.

phrases.t: Lo que sí podríamos hacer es adelantar una parte.
phrases.n: What we could do is deliver part of it earlier.

lessons.title: Reported speech: passing on both sides
lessons.goal: Report positions and requests neutrally, as a mediator would, with the right tense shifts.

tip.title: Dice que… / Dijo que…
tip.body: As a mediator you pass on positions without taking sides. With a present reporting verb (dice, asegura, afirma) the tenses stay as they were: Dice que está dispuesta a dialogar. With a past reporting verb (dijo, aseguró, comentó) they usually shift back: está → estaba, ha hablado → había hablado, vendrá → vendría, puede → podía. Reported requests and suggestions take que + subjunctive: present after dice/pide (Pide que le enviemos el contrato), imperfect subjunctive after dijo/pidió (Pidió que le enviáramos el contrato; -ase forms like enviásemos are equally correct). Yes/no questions are reported with si: Preguntó si podíamos firmar hoy. Neutral verbs like afirmar, sostener, reconocer and negar keep you impartial.

story.title: Entre dos frentes
story.intro: In Monterrey, a mediator passes on a team member's complaint to her manager, Mr Treviño.

lines.name: Patricia
lines.t: Licenciado Treviño, gracias por venir. Ayer hablé con Mariana y me pidió que le transmitiera su punto de vista.
lines.n: Mr Treviño, thank you for coming. Yesterday I spoke with Mariana and she asked me to pass on her point of view to you.
lines.note: Mexico: Licenciado/Licenciada is a common title for graduates.

lines.name: Sr. Treviño
lines.t: Adelante. Aunque, la verdad, no entiendo muy bien cuál es el problema.
lines.n: Go ahead. Although, to be honest, I don't really understand what the problem is.

lines.name: Patricia
lines.t: Ella siente que la dejan fuera de las decisiones. Dice que del cambio de horarios se enteró por un correo.
lines.n: She feels left out of decisions. She says she found out about the change of schedule from an email.

lines.name: Sr. Treviño
lines.t: Bueno, es que había prisa. Pero ella sabe que su trabajo es muy valioso para nosotros.
lines.n: Well, we were in a hurry. But she knows her work is very valuable to us.

lines.name: Patricia
lines.t: Eso tampoco lo niega. Reconoce que usted siempre la ha apoyado. Lo que le dolió fue la forma, no la decisión.
lines.n: She doesn't deny that either. She acknowledges that you've always supported her. What hurt her was the way it was done, not the decision.

lines.name: Sr. Treviño
lines.t: Mmm. Entiendo. ¿Y usted qué propone?
lines.n: Hmm. I see. And what do you suggest?

lines.name: Patricia
lines.t: Ayudaría explicar abiertamente los motivos de las decisiones importantes. Y propongo una reunión entre los tres, el jueves, si le parece.
lines.n: It would help to explain the reasons for important decisions openly. And I suggest a meeting with the three of us, on Thursday, if that suits you.

lines.name: Sr. Treviño
lines.t: De acuerdo, el jueves a las diez. Y que conste que no fue con mala intención.
lines.n: All right, Thursday at ten. And for the record, it wasn't done with bad intentions.

branch.title: Ciudades hermanas

lessons.title: Feedback and mediation in your words
lessons.goal: Give tactful feedback freely for a minute and a half.

culture.title: Small words that soften
culture.body: Diminutives soften requests and make them sound friendlier: ¿Me esperas un momentito?, ¿Me haces un favorcito? They are used everywhere, but especially often in Mexico and much of Latin America. In Mexico, ahorita (literally 'right now') can mean anything from 'this second' to 'later, maybe'. In Colombia, many people use usted even with friends and family, so it doesn't necessarily signal distance there. In Spain, tú is used more readily, and politeness tends to come from tone, the conditional and the imperfect: Quería pedirte un favor.

free.n: Give tactful feedback to a colleague whose reports keep arriving late. Show appreciation, describe the problem without judging, ask for their view and propose a solution.
free.hint: Quería comentarte una cosa… / Valoro mucho… / He notado que… / No te lo digo como un reproche… / ¿Tú cómo lo ves? / ¿Qué te parece si…?
free.model: Marta, quería comentarte una cosa. Valoro mucho tu compromiso con el equipo, y en general tu trabajo me parece excelente. Pero he notado que últimamente los informes llegan con algunos días de retraso. No te lo digo como un reproche, ni mucho menos. ¿Tú cómo lo ves? ¿Hay algo que te lo esté poniendo difícil? ¿Qué te parece si a partir de ahora dedicamos diez minutos cada lunes a repasar las prioridades?
